title: Modulation scaling curves
takeaway: Told to think about a concept while producing unrelated text, the model puts that concept at the top of the J-lens readout on most trials, and the rate tends to rise from Haiku to Sonnet to Opus. Told to ignore the concept, the model keeps the rate well below the focus level but not at zero, while the no-instruction baseline sits at approximately zero.
walkthrough:
This is the quantitative summary of the [[directed-modulation]] experiments: many trials of the covert tasks that section 3.2 first showed as single-prompt examples. In the article it is a live widget, titled "Directed modulation: instructed vs. suppressed activation", with two line-chart panels side by side and hoverable series.

Each panel is one instruction condition. The left panel is "Think about X", the focus condition; the right is "Ignore X", which names the concept but frames it as irrelevant. The horizontal axis of both panels is model size, ordered by tier: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, the ascending sizes of the [[claude-model-family]]. The vertical axis, labeled "Lens readout reflects target", runs 0 to 100%: how often the instructed target concept shows up in the [[jacobian-lens]] readout while the model's visible output is unrelated text. Each point averages over five to eight phrasings of the same instruction, so a point reflects the instruction type rather than one wording.

Three lines per panel give the task families. Category instance and math expression are versions of the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]] — hold a category member in mind, or mentally evaluate an expression, while copying an unrelated sentence — and a trial counts as positive if the target reaches J-lens top-1 at any (layer, position). Line width is the [[character-counting-task]]: silently count the characters in each line of a passage. Its measure is precision, the fraction of top-1 numeric readouts matching the true width.

Under focus, category and math run high — from 92.6% and 73.0% on Haiku up to 97.1% and 95.6% on Opus — and the paper reads this rise as a tendency to increase with model size, a trend resting on three points. Line width is much lower and non-monotonic (19.4%, 39.6%, 32.8%); the appendix attributes this to the task being harder both to perform and to specify. Under ignore, every family drops well below its focus level, yet category and math stay far above the no-instruction baseline, which the text reports as approximately zero and which the figure does not plot. Naming a concept in order to dismiss it still activates it, which the paper likens to the human [[white-bear-effect]]. The appendix adds that control is phrasing-sensitive: a bare mention primes the concept almost as strongly as a focus instruction.

terms.term: Directed modulation: instructed vs. suppressed activation
terms.definition: The widget's on-page title: the figure contrasts how strongly an instruction to hold a concept in mind loads it into the workspace against how well an instruction to ignore it keeps it out.
The focus condition: the prompt tells the model directly what to hold in mind (for example "concentrate on citrus fruits") while it copies or reads unrelated text.
The negative condition: the prompt names the target but frames it as irrelevant to the task ("X is irrelevant to this task"). It asks the model to keep the concept out of mind rather than in.
The 0–100% success measure: for category and math, the fraction of trials on which the target concept appears at top-1 in the J-lens readout; for line width, the precision of top-1 numeric readouts.
The size tier of the model under test, smallest to largest: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. Parameter counts are not disclosed; only the tier ordering carries meaning.
The smallest model tier in the comparison, the leftmost point on the size axis.
The middle model tier, and the paper's default subject model for most experiments.
The largest model tier in the comparison, the rightmost point on the size axis.
Trials in which the model is instructed to hold an instance of a named category in mind while copying an unrelated sentence, with the lens read at the copied tokens.
Trials in which the model is instructed to mentally evaluate an arithmetic expression (such as 3² − 2) while copying an unrelated sentence; the target is the expression's value.
Trials in which the model silently counts the characters in each line of a multi-line passage while reading it; the target is the line's character count, read at the newline token.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token in the J-lens readout at a given layer and position. For category and math, a trial is positive if the target token reaches top-1 anywhere.
One cell of the readout grid: one of the model's layers at one token position. The positive-trial criterion scans all such cells, so the target may surface at any depth and any token.

For the line-width family only: the fraction of top-1 number tokens in the lens readout that match the true character count of the line. A top-1-anywhere criterion would be too loose for a task whose answer is one number among many near misses like 39 or 41.
The five to eight alternative wordings instantiating each instruction condition; each plotted point is the average over these phrasings, hiding a spread the appendix shows separately.

Trials with the same surface task and no mental instruction, measuring whether the prompt context alone puts the target in the lens readout. The text reports its rate as approximately zero; the figure does not plot it as a panel.
One prompt instance: one stimulus, one instruction phrasing, one model. The plotted rates are fractions of trials.

numbers.meaning: Category-instance success under the focus instruction, for Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. The easiest family: on nearly every trial the held-in-mind category member reaches J-lens top-1 somewhere, and the rate creeps up with model size.

Math-expression success under focus, by ascending model size. The steepest size trend of the three families: the mentally computed value reaches top-1 far more reliably in the larger models. This is the clearest support for the paper's claim that focus-condition rates tend to increase with size.

Line-width precision under focus, by ascending model size — much lower than the other families and non-monotonic (Sonnet beats Opus). The appendix explains that this task is harder to perform (a running character count must be silently maintained) and to specify (phrasings range from "count the characters" to "figure out the column number").

Category-instance rate under the ignore instruction, by ascending model size: well below the 92–97% focus levels, but far above the near-zero baseline. Naming the concept in order to dismiss it still loads it on a substantial fraction of trials, and more so in the larger models.
Math-expression rate under ignore, by ascending model size — the same pattern as category: suppression works only partially, and residual activation is higher in Sonnet and Opus than in Haiku.

Line-width precision under ignore, by ascending model size: essentially at floor. When the count is framed as irrelevant, correct counts almost never reach top-1 — consistent with a task that must be actively performed, not merely primed.

The no-instruction baseline rate, reported in the text for all families and sizes. It shows the prompt context alone does not place the target in the lens readout, so any presence under the plotted conditions is attributable to the instruction.

The grid of the figure: three model sizes on the x-axis, three task-family lines, two instruction-condition panels. The appendix version adds two more conditions (mention and don't-think) that this main-text figure omits.
Phrasings per instruction condition; each plotted point is the mean over them, per the caption's note that each point averages over instruction phrasings.
The spread of Opus 4.5's line-width precision across individual focus phrasings, reported in the appendix — the sensitivity to wording that each averaged point in this figure hides.

The rank the target must reach, at some (layer, position), for a category or math trial to count as positive. Requiring the top rank makes the criterion strict: the concept must dominate the readout somewhere, not merely appear in it.
